$note:
Which application each namespace is emitted to. A namespace may appear under more than one target: it is still defined ONCE, in base/, and the generator writes the same entry to both catalogues, so the two cannot drift. That is the whole point of the single source — the old arrangement had 57 keys defined twice, 23 of them with different Spanish text, and which one a reader saw depended on lookup order.

Ownership is declared rather than inferred from a usage scan. A scan that misses a reference silently ships a catalogue without the key, and the miss surfaces to a customer; a declaration that is wrong is caught by verify-catalogues.mjs, which checks every referenced key against the catalogue its application actually receives.

client-web.$why: The browser renders all user-visible text, including the wording of every domain error: the server sends a code, a message key and its parameters, never prose, so the namespaces the API raises errors from are emitted here too. Excluded are the six the server renders itself with no browser in the loop -- transactional e-mail, the invoice PDF, the account and journal names written into a new tenant's books, the units those messages pluralise, the quota nouns in stored notifications, and the Electron menu. Shipping those to a browser would be ~300 keys per language that no screen can reach.
client-web.$core_why: The namespaces the application shell needs when a language chunk cannot be fetched at all. Emitted as <lang>.core.json and bundled, so a reader on a failing connection sees the sign-in page and the error wording rather than a screen of dotted identifiers. Everything else arrives with the language chunk.

api.$why: Every namespace. The API is a server: its catalogue is read from disk at boot and never shipped to a browser, so there is no size to trade against completeness, and two things need the whole thing. It renders text itself where no browser is in the loop -- transactional e-mail, the invoice PDF, the account and journal names written into a new tenant's books, stored notifications. And I18nExceptionFilter asks `i18n.has(key)` to decide whether a failure can name a specific message or has to fall back to the generic one for its status; a key the server cannot see would silently downgrade a precise message to "That request is not valid".

pos.$why: The till is a separate application with its own bundle, so it gets its own small catalogue rather than the whole product's. It shows its own screens, the shared error wording, and the generic confirmations.

desktop.$why: The Electron shell only draws a native menu; the rest of the window is the web client, which loads its own catalogue.
